questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has had exertional breathlessness and chest tightness for 6 months. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and slow-rising, and BP 122/90 mmHg. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids. An ECG is recorded (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Tall left-sided voltages with lateral T wave inversion: left ventricular hypertrophy with strain.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her valve disease?
questions.e: In the elderly UK population, aortic stenosis is most commonly caused by degenerative calcification; the ECG shows LVH.

steps.x: **Elderly** with an AS murmur and LVH.

elim: No fever or embolic features; causes regurgitation more than stenosis.
Causes aortic root dilation and regurgitation.
Less common in the UK and usually affects the mitral valve too.

steps.x: **B. Degenerative calcification.** Elderly AS = degenerative calcification; younger = bicuspid.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman who grew up in rural India has 2 years of increasing breathlessness and fatigue. She remembers months of joint pains and a heart problem aged 11. Her pulse is collapsing, rate 86 bpm and BP 158/46 mmHg. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her valve lesion?
questions.e: Worldwide, aortic regurgitation is most commonly caused by rheumatic heart disease, often after childhood rheumatic fever.

clues: joint pains and a heart problem aged 11
steps.x: AR + **childhood rheumatic fever**.

elim: No tall stature or lens dislocation described.

steps.x: **E. Rheumatic heart disease.** AR worldwide: rheumatic heart disease.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man who injects drugs has had fevers and night sweats for 3 weeks. He is now breathless. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 136/48 mmHg. There are splinter haemorrhages and a new high-pitched blowing early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
questions.q: Which is the most likely valve lesion?
questions.e: Infective endocarditis destroying the aortic valve causes regurgitation: an early diastolic blowing murmur and wide pulse pressure.

clues: early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
steps.x: **Early diastolic**, **left sternal edge**, wide pulse pressure.

elim: Gives an ejection systolic murmur and narrow pulse pressure.
Low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex.
Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge with giant v waves.

steps.x: **A. Aortic regurgitation.** AR causes include infective endocarditis.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has had chest tightness when climbing stairs, breathlessness on exertion, and an episode of feeling faint while gardening. His pulse rate is 70 bpm, BP 128/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His GP suspects a valve problem.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation?
o: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
questions.e: Angina, presyncope and exertional dyspnoea is the classic aortic stenosis triad; the murmur is ejection systolic at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids.

steps.x: **Angina + syncope + dyspnoea**: the AS triad.
**C. Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.** AS: ESM at right 2nd ICS radiating to carotids.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman with exertional angina has an ejection systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space radiating to both carotids. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 118/96 mmHg. Her GP palpates the precordium and the carotid pulse.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding?
o: Systolic thrill with a slow-rising carotid pulse
questions.e: Aortic stenosis gives a slow-rising, narrow pulse pressure pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a systolic thrill.

steps.x: AS murmur with **narrow pulse pressure**.
**D. Systolic thrill with a slow-rising carotid pulse.** AS: pulsus parvus et tardus and systolic thrill.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has chronic aortic regurgitation from a bicuspid aortic valve. He has mild exertional breathlessness, fatigue and palpitations. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and collapsing. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
questions.q: Which is the most likely blood pressure reading?
questions.e: Aortic regurgitation gives a wide pulse pressure because diastolic pressure falls as blood runs back into the ventricle.

steps.x: AR: **wide pulse pressure**.

elim: Narrow pulse pressure, as in aortic stenosis.
Diastolic hypertension, not wide pulse pressure.
Hypotension without a wide pulse pressure.

steps.x: **D. 168/44 mmHg.** AR: soft S1, wide pulse pressure, collapsing pulse.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a 1 year history of breathlessness, fatigue and palpitations. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and collapsing, and BP 162/48 mmHg. The first heart sound is soft. Echocardiography later shows a dilated left ventricle with diastolic backflow across the aortic valve.
questions.q: Which is the most likely murmur?
o: Ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge
High-pitched early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex
Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge
questions.e: Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic, high-pitched, blowing murmur best heard at the left sternal edge.

clues: diastolic backflow across the aortic valve
steps.x: Wide pulse pressure and **diastolic backflow**: AR.
**B. High-pitched early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.** AR murmur: early diastolic, left sternal edge.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has severe aortic regurgitation. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 170/40 mmHg. While he sits talking, his head bobs forward in time with each heartbeat. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
questions.q: Which is the name of the head movement?
questions.e: Head nodding with each heartbeat is De Musset's sign of aortic regurgitation.

clues: head bobs forward in time with each heartbeat
steps.x: **Head** nodding: De Musset's.

elim: A pistol-shot sound over the femoral artery.

steps.x: **B. De Musset's sign.** AR signs: Quincke's nails, Muller's uvula, De Musset's head, Corrigan's carotid.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with Marfan syndrome has aortic regurgitation. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 158/42 mmHg. When she opens her mouth, the uvula is seen to pulsate with each heartbeat. Her carotid pulses are visibly prominent.
questions.q: Which is the name of the uvula finding?
questions.e: Uvula pulsation is Muller's sign, an eponymous sign of aortic regurgitation.

steps.x: **Uvula**: Muller's.

elim: Bounding carotid, which she also has.
The collapsing pulse at the wrist.

steps.x: **C. Muller's sign.** Muller's = uvula pulsation in AR.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman has aortic stenosis and has become more breathless over 3 months. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and slow-rising, and BP 108/90 mmHg. There is an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Her cardiologist is assessing whether the stenosis is severe.
questions.q: Which examination finding would most indicate severe disease?
o: Murmur not radiating to the carotids
Soft or absent second heart sound
questions.e: Severe AS gives a soft or absent S2, often with an S4; echocardiography shows a gradient above 40 mmHg.

steps.x: Severity sign: a **quiet S2**.

elim: S2 becomes soft in severe AS.

steps.x: **D. Soft or absent second heart sound.** Severe AS: soft/absent S2, S4, gradient >40 mmHg.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with hypertension has sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He is pale and breathless. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 84/38 mmHg, with a difference between arms. There is a new early diastolic murmur and bilateral basal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his new murmur and shock?
o: Acute aortic regurgitation from aortic dissection
Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture
questions.e: Acute aortic regurgitation, most commonly from aortic dissection, presents with cardiogenic shock and acute heart failure.

clues: tearing chest pain radiating to his back
steps.x: **Tearing pain**, arm BP difference, **new AR murmur**, shock.

elim: Gives a pansystolic murmur after MI, not tearing back pain.
Muffled heart sounds and raised JVP, no diastolic murmur.
An ejection systolic murmur, not early diastolic.
No diastolic murmur or arm BP difference.

steps.x: **A. Acute aortic regurgitation from aortic dissection.** Acute AR: commonly aortic dissection; shock and heart failure.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has severe aortic regurgitation from rheumatic heart disease. His pulse is collapsing, BP 166/42 mmHg. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. His mitral valve is structurally normal on echocardiography.
questions.q: Which additional murmur is most likely heard at the apex?
o: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Late systolic murmur after a click
Opening snap followed by a diastolic rumble
Pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
questions.e: Severe AR can produce an Austin Flint murmur: a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex with a normal mitral valve.

steps.x: Severe AR + **normal mitral valve** + apical rumble.

elim: Organic mitral stenosis; the mitral valve is normal.

steps.x: **E. Rumbling mid-diastolic murmur.** Austin Flint murmur in severe AR.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has a soft ejection systolic murmur heard at a routine health check. He has no symptoms. His GP is trying to decide whether this is aortic stenosis or aortic sclerosis. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which finding would most support aortic stenosis?
questions.e: Aortic sclerosis gives an ESM that does not radiate to the carotids with normal S2, pulse character and volume.

steps.x: Sclerosis is **all normal** except the murmur; AS **radiates**.

elim: Typical of sclerosis; S2 is soft in severe AS.

steps.x: **A. Murmur radiating to the carotids.** Sclerosis: no carotid radiation, normal S2 and pulse.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension has increasing breathlessness. His pulse is collapsing, BP 172/52 mmHg. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Echocardiography shows structurally normal valve leaflets and an aortic root diameter of 4.9 cm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his valve lesion?
questions.e: A dilated aortic root stretches the annulus so normal leaflets cannot coapt, causing aortic regurgitation.

steps.x: Normal leaflets, **big root**.

elim: Causes stenosis, and leaflets are normal.

steps.x: **A. Aortic root dilation.** AR causes: rheumatic, root dilation, endocarditis, Marfan's.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has breathlessness on exertion. Echocardiography shows the aortic valve leaflets fail to close in diastole, with a jet of blood flowing from the aorta back into the left ventricle. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 150/50 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Aortic regurgitation is failure of the aortic valve to close, so blood leaks back into the left ventricle.

steps.x: Aortic valve **fails to close**: backflow into LV.

elim: Backflow from LV to left atrium in systole.

steps.x: **A. Aortic regurgitation.** AS obstructs outflow; AR leaks back.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman has exertional breathlessness and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/92 mmHg. Transthoracic echocardiography is performed.
questions.q: Which echocardiography finding would most indicate severe aortic stenosis?
questions.e: Echocardiography grades AS by pressure gradient; a gradient above 40 mmHg indicates severe stenosis.

clues: ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
steps.x: Severity on echo: **gradient > 40 mmHg**.

elim: Normal and not a measure of stenosis.
Not a measure of AS severity.

steps.x: **E. Peak trans-valvular gradient of 58 mmHg.** Severe AS: gradient >40 mmHg.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has had increasing fatigue and breathlessness. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and collapsing, and BP 156/50 mmHg. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. His chest X-ray shows mild cardiomegaly.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Transthoracic echocardiography is the definitive investigation and shows valve structure and degree of regurgitation.

steps.x: Suspected AR: **image the valve**.

elim: Not first; echo is gold standard.
Assesses coronary arteries, not valve regurgitation.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiogram.** TTE is gold standard for AS and AR.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man with known severe aortic stenosis has worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea and ankle swelling. His pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 112/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. There are bibasal crackles. A chest X-ray is taken (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Enlarged cardiac silhouette with bilateral alveolar oedema.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the chest X-ray?
questions.e: In decompensated AS the chest X-ray may show cardiomegaly and pulmonary oedema.

steps.x: Decompensated AS: **heart failure** on CXR.

elim: No sudden pleuritic pain or absent breath sounds.

steps.x: **B. Cardiomegaly with pulmonary oedema.** CXR: cardiomegaly and pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man attends his GP with exertional chest tightness. There is an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 130/94 mmHg. An urgent echocardiogram is requested.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to perform in the surgery today?
questions.e: An ECG is done first-line and in AS typically shows left ventricular hypertrophy; echo is the definitive test.

steps.x: Quick first test before echo: **ECG** for LVH.

elim: Invasive and not a primary-care test.
For intermittent arrhythmia, not valve disease.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** ECG first-line (LVH); TTE definitive.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with Marfan syndrome is well with no chest pain. Echocardiography shows mild aortic regurgitation and an aortic root diameter of 4.7 cm. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate follow-up?
questions.e: Aortic root 4.5 to 5.4 cm: 3-monthly ultrasound; below 4.5 cm yearly; symptoms or above 5.5 cm surgery.

steps.x: **4.7 cm**, asymptomatic: the 4.5-5.4 cm band.

elim: The root is dilated and needs surveillance.
For symptoms or diameter above 5.5 cm.

steps.x: **C. Ultrasound every 3 months.** Root 4.5-5.4 cm: 3-monthly ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with a bicuspid aortic valve has an echocardiogram at a routine clinic. The aortic root measures 4.2 cm. He has no symptoms. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. The valve gradient is 24 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate surveillance of his aortic root?
questions.e: An aortic root below 4.5 cm is followed with yearly ultrasound.

steps.x: **Below 4.5 cm**: yearly.
**E. Yearly ultrasound.** Root <4.5 cm: yearly ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man with Marfan syndrome has had 3-monthly surveillance of a dilated aortic root. Today it measures 5.7 cm. He has no chest pain. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Endovascular stent of the abdominal aorta
questions.e: An aortic root above 5.5 cm or a symptomatic root needs open surgical repair.

steps.x: **Above 5.5 cm**: operate.
**C. Refer for open surgical repair.** Symptomatic or >5.5 cm: open surgical repair.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has severe aortic stenosis on echocardiography but says she has no symptoms. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/94 mmHg. The cardiologist reviews further echocardiography and blood results to decide whether to refer for valve replacement.
questions.q: Which result would most indicate referral for aortic valve replacement?
o: BNP 1.2 times the upper limit of normal
questions.e: AVR referral in severe AS: Vmax above 5 m/s, valve area below 0.6 cm², LVEF below 55%, BNP over 2x ULN, or symptoms on exercise testing.

steps.x: Asymptomatic severe AS: look for a **threshold** crossed.
**E. Peak jet velocity of 5.3 m/s.** Vmax >5, area <0.6, EF <55%, BNP >2x ULN.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with severe aortic stenosis reports no symptoms. During a supervised exercise test he becomes breathless and his BP falls from 138/88 mmHg to 112/80 mmHg. His LVEF is 60%. He is otherwise fit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Symptoms unmasked on exercise testing in severe AS are an indication for valve replacement.

steps.x: Exercise **unmasked symptoms**.
**B. Refer for aortic valve replacement.** Symptomatic severe AS: AVR.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a soft ejection systolic murmur. Echocardiography shows mild aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 18 mmHg and normal left ventricular function. She has no symptoms. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Mild, asymptomatic aortic stenosis is managed with regular cardiology follow-up and monitoring.

steps.x: **Mild** and **asymptomatic**: watch.

elim: Only for severe or symptomatic disease.
Aortic stenosis progresses and needs monitoring.

steps.x: **C. Regular cardiology outpatient follow-up.** Mild asymptomatic AS: outpatient monitoring.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man with severe aortic stenosis is awaiting TAVI. He has developed ankle swelling, orthopnoea and bibasal crackles. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 116/90 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. His weight has risen by 3 kg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms while he waits?
questions.e: Diuretics such as furosemide give symptomatic relief of fluid overload; heart failure is managed as complications arise.

steps.x: **Fluid overload**: a loop diuretic.

elim: Vasodilators can drop BP dangerously in AS and do not treat fluid overload.
Not for fluid overload in sinus rhythm.
Vasodilation is hazardous with fixed outflow obstruction.

steps.x: **C. Furosemide.** Furosemide for symptomatic fluid overload.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man had a mechanical aortic valve replacement for a bicuspid valve 2 weeks ago. He is starting long-term warfarin and aspirin. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. There is a crisp metallic second heart sound.
questions.q: Which is the target INR?
questions.e: A mechanical aortic valve needs lifelong warfarin with a target INR of 3.0, plus long-term aspirin.

steps.x: Mechanical valve: warfarin **INR 3.0**.

elim: Too low for a mechanical aortic valve in the notes.

steps.x: **C. 3.0.** Mechanical valve: target INR 3.0 + aspirin.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 66 mmHg. She is fit for open surgery. She had a major gastrointestinal bleed on anticoagulation 2 years ago and her gastroenterologist advises against lifelong anticoagulation. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: A mechanical valve is contraindicated when anticoagulation is contraindicated; a fit patient under 75 can have a bioprosthetic valve.

steps.x: Fit, under 75, **cannot anticoagulate**.

elim: Needs lifelong warfarin, which is contraindicated.
Severe symptomatic AS needs valve replacement.
For high-risk patients, typically over 80; she is fit for surgery.

steps.x: **B. Bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement.** Bioprosthetic: under 75, fit; mechanical needs warfarin.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is awaiting surgical aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis. Last month he had transient weakness of his right hand and slurred speech lasting 30 minutes. Carotid Doppler shows 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 136/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which additional procedure is most likely to be needed?
questions.e: Patients with coexisting carotid disease may need carotid endarterectomy alongside valve surgery.

clues: 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery
steps.x: Symptomatic **carotid stenosis** in an AVR patient.
**A. Carotid endarterectomy.** Coexisting carotid disease: carotid endarterectomy.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has had a mechanical aortic valve for 6 years and takes warfarin with stable INRs. He has read that newer anticoagulants need no blood tests and asks to switch to apixaban. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop anticoagulation and take aspirin alone
Switch to low molecular weight heparin long term
questions.e: Any mechanical heart valve requires lifelong warfarin; DOACs are not suitable.

steps.x: **Mechanical valve**: warfarin only.

elim: DOACs are not used with mechanical valves.
DOACs are not used with mechanical valves.

steps.x: **A. Continue warfarin lifelong.** Mechanical valve = lifelong warfarin.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with known severe aortic stenosis collapsed while walking up a hill and lost consciousness for a few seconds. She now feels well. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm, BP 118/96 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. There is an ejection systolic murmur with a soft second heart sound.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Syncope in known or critical aortic stenosis is a red flag requiring urgent assessment.

steps.x: **Exertional syncope** + **severe AS**: red flag.

elim: Too slow for exertional syncope in severe AS.
Exertional syncope in AS is a red flag.

steps.x: **E. Urgent same-day cardiology assessment.** Syncope in AS = urgent assessment.

questions.stem: An 85 year old woman has severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 72 mmHg. She had coronary bypass surgery 10 years ago, has severe COPD and is judged too high risk for open surgery. She lives independently. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 120/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: TAVI is used for less fit, higher-risk patients, typically over 80.

clues: too high risk for open surgery
steps.x: Over 80, **high surgical risk**: TAVI.

elim: Needs open surgery, too high risk.
Open surgery and lifelong warfarin at 85.
Severe symptomatic AS benefits from valve replacement.

steps.x: **E. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation.** Severe or symptomatic AS (>40 mmHg): AVR; TAVI if high risk.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has had chronic aortic regurgitation for many years. Echocardiography shows a large, dilated left ventricle with normal wall thickness relative to its size. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 164/46 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the ventricular change?
questions.e: Diastolic backflow volume-overloads the LV, causing eccentric hypertrophy and dilation.

steps.x: AR = **volume** overload; AS = **pressure** overload.

elim: Gives thick walls and small cavity.
Regional wall motion loss, no history of MI.

steps.x: **E. Volume overload causing eccentric hypertrophy.** AR: eccentric hypertrophy and dilation.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has aortic regurgitation. His BP is 170/38 mmHg and his radial pulse collapses suddenly when his arm is raised. His pulse rate is 84 bpm. A student asks why his diastolic pressure is so low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Rapid run-off of blood back into the left ventricle
questions.e: Wide pulse pressure in AR comes from low diastolic pressure due to rapid run-off back into the ventricle.

clues: why his diastolic pressure is so low
steps.x: Diastole: blood **leaks back**.

elim: Stroke volume is increased in AR.
Not the main cause of his low diastolic pressure.

steps.x: **C. Rapid run-off of blood back into the left ventricle.** AR: rapid run-off lowers diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman has severe calcific aortic stenosis. Her carotid pulse is small volume and slow to rise, and the second heart sound is barely audible. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 110/92 mmHg. A student asks why these signs occur.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: A fixed narrow orifice slows ejection and reduces valve closure sound
questions.e: The fixed narrowed orifice slows and reduces ejection velocity and the calcified valve barely moves, so S2 is soft.

steps.x: **Fixed, rigid** narrow valve.

elim: Muffles all heart sounds, not a slow-rising pulse.

steps.x: **A. A fixed narrow orifice slows ejection and reduces valve closure sound.** Severe AS: slow-rising pulse and soft S2.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has exertional breathlessness. Echocardiography shows a calcified, stenosed aortic valve with only two leaflets. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/90 mmHg. A student asks why he has stenosis decades earlier than most patients.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Congenital fusion causing a pinhole valve from birth
Turbulent flow causing accelerated fibrosis and calcification
questions.e: Abnormal bicuspid leaflet mechanics cause turbulent flow and accelerated fibrosis and calcification.

steps.x: **Bicuspid** = turbulence = early calcification.

elim: Rheumatic disease, not a bicuspid valve.
A bicuspid valve usually functions normally in childhood.

steps.x: **E. Turbulent flow causing accelerated fibrosis and calcification.** Bicuspid valve: earlier stenosis in younger patients.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has had severe aortic stenosis with left ventricular hypertrophy for years. Over 6 months he has developed orthopnoea and ankle swelling. Echocardiography now shows an ejection fraction of 35%. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 106/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his new heart failure?
o: Decompensation of the hypertrophied ventricle against a fixed afterload
questions.e: A fixed outflow obstruction causes compensatory concentric LVH, which eventually decompensates into heart failure.

steps.x: Years of **pressure load**, then failure.
**C. Decompensation of the hypertrophied ventricle against a fixed afterload.** AS: concentric LVH, then decompensation.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has severe aortic regurgitation. There is a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex, but echocardiography shows a normal mitral valve. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 160/44 mmHg. A student asks which valve lesion this murmur imitates and why.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: The aortic jet restricts mitral opening, mimicking mitral stenosis
questions.e: In the Austin Flint murmur the regurgitant jet interferes with mitral opening, functionally mimicking mitral stenosis.

steps.x: Normal mitral valve but an MS-like murmur: **functional**.

elim: Pansystolic at the lower left sternal edge.

steps.x: **D. The aortic jet restricts mitral opening, mimicking mitral stenosis.** Austin Flint: functional mitral stenosis from the AR jet.
